prompt: Two team lists record engineers who know Python and engineers who know Java. Some engineers appear on both. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adding the list sizes counts each bilingual engineer twice.
options.explanation: They contribute once to each list.

options.text: Adding the sizes always gives the number of distinct engineers on either list.
options.explanation: This is true only if the lists are disjoint.

options.text: Subtracting the overlap once gives the distinct count on at least one list.
options.explanation: It removes exactly the duplicate contribution.

options.text: To count those on neither list, subtract the union count from the whole team size.
options.explanation: The team splits into the union and its complement.

options.text: The overlap and the neither group always have the same size.
options.explanation: Membership in both and membership in neither are different conditions.

workedExample: Track a single bilingual engineer: adding lists gives two contributions, so subtract one. A person on exactly one list already contributes once and is not subtracted. A person on neither contributes zero. After correcting the union, the rest of the team is the neither group.

prompt: To count integers divisible by neither two nor three, a developer starts with the whole range and subtracts both sets of multiples. What needs correction?

options.text: Nothing: the removed sets never overlap.
options.explanation: Multiples of six belong to both removed sets.

options.text: Add back multiples of six once.
options.explanation: They were removed twice but must be removed only once.

options.text: Subtract multiples of six once more.
options.explanation: That would deepen the double subtraction.
Some odd numbers are multiples of three and must remain excluded.

workedExample: A multiple of six starts with one contribution, then loses one for each divisor group, leaving a negative contribution. Restoring it once brings it to zero, as required for an excluded integer. Integers divisible by neither retain their original single contribution.

prompt: For the union of three sets, you add each set size and subtract all three pairwise intersections. What happens to an element belonging to all three sets?

options.text: It is still counted three times.
options.explanation: The pairwise subtractions have removed three contributions.
Three additions and three subtractions leave no contribution.

options.text: It must be excluded from the union.
options.explanation: Belonging to all three certainly means belonging to at least one.

options.text: It is counted zero times, so the triple intersection must be added back once.
options.explanation: This restores its required single contribution.

workedExample: The element appears in each of the three original sets and each of their three pairwise intersections. The first two stages cancel all its contributions. Add the triple intersection once so it appears exactly once in the union.
